summary: Defines the Capabilities optional parameter for BGP-4, which lets two peers announce which new features they support when a session starts. This allows new features to be introduced gracefully without tearing down peering sessions. It obsoletes RFC 3392.

plainLanguage.summary: When two people meet, they might say which languages they speak. This note lets two routers tell each other which special features they understand, without having to hang up and start again.

questions: what is the bgp capabilities parameter
how do bgp peers negotiate features
subtitle: How two BGP routers tell each other which optional features they support, without dropping the session.

tldr.problem: Base BGP-4 says a speaker must terminate the peering if an OPEN message has an unrecognized Optional Parameter, which makes introducing new capabilities hard.
tldr.mechanism: A Capabilities Optional Parameter (type 2) in the OPEN message lists capabilities as code, length and value triples. A capability is used only if both peers advertised it, and unknown capabilities are ignored.
tldr.outcome: New BGP features can be introduced gracefully without tearing down peering. RFC 5492 obsoletes RFC 3392 and has been updated by RFC 8810.

today: RFC 5492 is a Draft Standard published in February 2009. It obsoletes RFC 3392 and has been updated by RFC 8810.

sections.title: Why Capabilities Are Needed
sections.content:
The base BGP-4 specification (RFC 4271) requires that when a speaker gets an OPEN message with one or more unrecognized Optional Parameters, it must terminate the BGP peering. That makes it hard to add new capabilities to BGP.

RFC 5492 defines an Optional Parameter and processing rules so speakers can communicate capabilities in an OPEN message. Two speakers that support it can establish a peering even when shown unrecognized capabilities, as long as all capabilities required to support the peering are supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, a router that heard something it did not understand would hang up. Now routers can mention extra things, and the other side simply skips what it does not know.

sections.title: How Advertisement Works
sections.content:
A speaker that supports capabilities advertisement MAY include a Capabilities Optional Parameter in its OPEN message, listing what it supports. It learns what its peer supports from the OPEN message it receives. Put simply, a capability can be used on a peering if both peers advertised it.

If a speaker sends the parameter and gets a NOTIFICATION with the Error Subcode Unsupported Optional Parameter, the peer does not support capabilities advertisement. The speaker SHOULD then try to re-establish the connection without sending the parameter.

A speaker that receives a capability it does not recognise MUST ignore it. It MUST NOT send an Unsupported Capability NOTIFICATION or terminate the session because of it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router shows a list of tricks it knows. They only use the tricks that are on both lists, and ignore any trick they have never heard of.

sections.title: The Capabilities Optional Parameter
sections.content:
The Capabilities parameter has Parameter Type 2. It holds one or more triples of Capability Code (one octet), Capability Length (one octet, the length of the value in octets) and Capability Value (variable, interpreted by the code).

Speakers SHOULD NOT include more than one instance of a capability with the same code, length and value, but MUST be prepared to accept duplicates. A speaker MAY include several instances with the same code and different values, and how those are processed must be described by the document that introduces the capability.

The parameter SHOULD appear in the OPEN message only once, with all capabilities as TLVs inside it. For backward compatibility, a speaker MUST accept several Capabilities parameters in one OPEN and treat the capabilities the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Each trick is written as a short card: a number saying which trick, how long the details are, and the details. All the cards go in one envelope.

sections.title: The Unsupported Capability Error
sections.content:
RFC 5492 defines the NOTIFICATION Error Subcode Unsupported Capability, with value 7. Its Data field MUST list the capabilities that caused the message, each encoded as in the OPEN message.

A speaker that needs a capability its peer lacks MAY send this NOTIFICATION and end the peering. The example given is a peering set up to exchange IPv6 routes where the peer does not support Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4 (RFC 4760). That decision is local to the speaker, and such a peering SHOULD NOT be re-established automatically. The message MUST NOT be used merely because an unknown capability was received.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router really needs a trick the other one lacks, it can say so and leave. It must not leave just because the other one mentioned a trick it did not know.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA maintains the Capability Code registry. Code 0 is reserved. Codes 1 through 63 are assigned by IETF Review, 64 through 127 by First Come First Served, and 128 through 255 are for Private Use.

IANA also maintains the "BGP OPEN Optional Parameter Types" registry, with 0 reserved and 1 to 255 allocated by IETF Review. It lists Parameter Type 1 (Authentication, deprecated) and Parameter Type 2 (Capabilities).
sections.plainLanguage: A keeper of the list hands out the numbers for each trick, so two different tricks never share one number.

sections.title: Security and Changes from RFC 3392
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section says this extension does not change the underlying security issues inherent in BGP, and refers to RFC 4272.

Compared with RFC 3392, this document makes minor editorial changes, updates references, clarifies use of the Unsupported Optional Parameter NOTIFICATION, clarifies behaviour when the Capabilities parameter appears multiple times in an OPEN message, and changes a number of SHOULDs to MUSTs.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling each other about tricks does not make the conversation any safer or less safe than before. This version mostly cleans up unclear rules.
